items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I was in Benny Goodman’s band.

ctx.x: Do you know anything about his training in Italy, how he became a musician?

He knew every aria from every opera. He studied – I was a legit performer myself. When they call me a jazz drummer, I smile, because I was brought up with the opera – all the opera [?], and classical music. Of course, Dad having a music store, I got all the records – the jazz records that came in from Louis Armstrong, Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Lionel Hampton, Cab Calloway. I knew all those records when I was a kid.
Francine said earlier that you only spoke Italian when you were a bambino. So Italian was spoken in the house?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: I was very fortunate. They looked at my credentials, having worked with Benny Goodman. ... And that’s what happened. ... it was a great experience joining Benny’s band. ... Yeah I did just under a year with Benny

ctx.x: Well you went through a real succession of great big bands and you must have been popular, because you hit them all.

I was very fortunate. Back home, when I was fourteen, fifteen, sixteen years old, there used to be a couple of places, one in Moline and one in Davenport, where all the big bands came to play the big ballrooms. The Coliseum in Davenport in particular, and every time a band like Ted Weems or Harry James or Ted Fio Rito, I’m naming some of the old guys now, all the kids would say “hey, let Louie play the drums” you know. So the band leader would always say “yeah, okay, where is he?” And I’d get up and I’d play you…
You were what, seventeen or something?
